title: Comfort for their baby
topic: End of life, DNACPR and ceilings of care
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on the antenatal ward. At 22 weeks, the fetal medicine team diagnosed a severe heart condition in Mr and Mrs Bennett's baby, which they explained is very likely to be life-limiting after birth. The couple have decided to continue the pregnancy.

Today, during a routine check, Mrs Bennett asks you, "What will happen to our baby when she's born? Will she be in pain?"
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Suggest they reconsider their decision to continue the pregnancy.
options.brief: Undermines a decision they have made.
options.detailed: They have made their decision with the fetal medicine team. Revisiting it now isn't supportive or appropriate.

options.text: Ask them what they have been told and what matters most to them.
options.brief: Their understanding and hopes shape any plan.
options.detailed: They may already have information, or have specific worries. Knowing what matters to them, such as time together, helps the team plan care that reflects their wishes.

options.text: Arrange for them to meet the neonatal palliative care team.
options.brief: Specialist teams can plan comfort care with them.
options.detailed: Perinatal palliative care teams can explain what may happen and plan for their baby's comfort, including pain relief. This is the right team to answer their questions in detail.

options.text: Reassure them that their baby may well be fine after birth.
options.detailed: The prognosis has been explained as very likely life-limiting. False reassurance could make things harder.

options.text: Tell them there is nothing that can be done for their baby.
options.brief: Untrue: comfort and support can be planned.
options.detailed: Even when cure isn't possible, much can be done to keep their baby comfortable and support the family.

options.text: Say the fetal medicine team will answer their questions at the next appointment.
options.brief: Defers their concern without any support now.
options.detailed: The specialist team should give detail, but deferring entirely leaves them without any response today.

options.text: Offer support from the bereavement midwife.
options.brief: Specialist emotional support for this situation.
options.detailed: Bereavement midwives support families through life-limiting diagnoses, including planning and memory-making. Offering this shows care for them as parents.

options.text: Explain in detail what usually happens to babies with this condition.
options.brief: Beyond your knowledge, and may not apply to their baby.
options.detailed: Specialists should explain this. General information from you may be inaccurate or upsetting.

explanation.issue: This tests how you support parents facing a life-limiting diagnosis for their baby, compassionately and within your role.
explanation.keyDetails: The diagnosis is very likely life-limiting. They have decided to continue the pregnancy. They are asking about comfort and pain.
explanation.reasoning: [B] learns their understanding and wishes, [C] brings in the teams who can plan care, and [G] offers emotional support. The distractors are directive ([A]), falsely reassuring ([D]), inaccurate ([E]), deferring ([F]), or beyond your role ([H]).
explanation.competing: [F] would be right if specialist help weren't available, but the planning teams can be involved now.

references.title: Treatment and care towards the end of life: good practice in decision making
references.note: Care towards the end of life, including for babies, and supporting families.
